pages.text: Down in Hazelwood somebody is coughing. Then somebody else. A dry, barking cough, house after house, like dogs answering each other. The children first, as always. Half the school is empty.
Wren the healer comes up the hill with a basket on each arm. “I cannot do this alone, {player},” she says, as if it costs her a tooth. “Berit had a still-room, behind your kitchen. Would you look?”

Somebody has swept the still-room floor in small, careful circles, but never quite to the end. The footprints in the dust are wide, flat, patient-looking. The kettle on the hearth is cold, its lid off, as if somebody was about to make tea and was interrupted.
Under the last shelf lies a page, torn in two. The top half is in a tidy hand: “Tea first. Always tea first.” The bottom half is missing. Somebody was here before you, and cared.
Wren is waiting at the edge of the forest with her arms folded. “One rule,” she says. “Bring me your basket. Every time. Before you use anything in it.”

“Plants have twins, and some twins are poison. I do not care how clever you are. I care that you wake up tomorrow.” She almost smiles. “It costs a little favour. A biscuit will do, or a bucket of water.”

c5_conch.title: Something white
c5_conch.text: Far off between the trees, something white and spiral shines in the green. It does not move. You hold your breath. Then you go back to your basket. Some things are for later.

c5_first_tea.title: A pupil for Wren
c5_first_tea.text: Greenstem, the boy from the market, stands in the doorway of the still-room and sniffs. “Can I learn this?” Wren grumbles something about boys and mud. Then she says yes.

pages.text: The ceiling. A blanket. A cup of something bitter. Wren sits by your bed, and she is not smiling. “What were you thinking?” she says. Your purse is gone. Your legs shake.
“You are well,” she says. “That is all that matters. Next time, the basket comes to me first.” She puts a hand on your head, very briefly, and goes to stir her pot.

c5_page.title: The other half
c5_page.text: The chest is full. In its lid, rolled up, you find the other half of the torn page: “The badger left after the fever, when nobody let the children rest.” You read it twice. You were one of those children.

pages.text: You make one more tea, and one more, day and night. Then the pot tilts and the floor comes up. Wren finds you on the stone. “You never stop, do you?” she says, and carries you to the bench.

Later, half awake, you say one thing. “The bucket's empty.” “What bucket?” says Wren. “By the door,” says Greenstem from the doorway. “Under the hook. It is always full.” Wren fills the dented bucket and sets it by your bench. She asks nothing at all.

At the still-room door sits a badger, very upright, the way somebody sits who has come about something important. He is old and grey and striped, and he smells of dried herbs. On his nose are small, round spectacles.

He looks at the healer's chest. He looks at the tea set. He looks at your face, and at your hands, which are shaking a little. He sets the empty cup in front of you, pours, and sits down on the other side of the table.

Tea first, says the look. For once you do nothing at all. The steam goes up from two cups in two thin lines. A line of the old rhyme comes back: “Wise badger heals what aches and stings.” The badger lifts his cup a little. Yes. Obviously.

Rain. A boy runs up the hill with a letter, dripping. The seal is red wax, pressed with a heavy ring. The face on the ring looks as if it has had a very long day. “From the Lord, from the Hurst,” he pants. “Right into your hand.”
You take it. You do not open it. You put it on the table. The badger looks at it over his spectacles. Then he looks at you. He says nothing. He puts the kettle on.
“Did you get better?” asks Minena. “Badgers make very slow tea,” you say. “By the time it was ready, I was.” Somebody laughs. Somebody yawns. Somebody asks if badgers have teapots.
“And the letter?” asks Minena. “From the Lord? What did it say?” You look at the window for a long time. “I did not open it,” you say. “Not that night.”
